newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway crown plunges, investors seen overreacting.
newsitem.headline: Norway crown plunges, investors seen overreacting.

text.p: Foreign investors pulled the plug on the Norwegian crown this week, sending it to four-month lows against the German mark and a basket of European currencies.

Analysts believe lower oil prices, wage talks later this month and high Norwegian CPI figures had prompted some players, including U.S. funds, to sell. Investors may also have thought the crown would not strengthen any further and had exhausted its potential, they said.

"This is an overreaction by the market," said Nils Gunnar Bratlie of bond sales at Chase Manhattan Bank in Oslo. "I think the crown will appreciate again in the longer term on the basis of strong fundamentals."
Norway's March CPI rose 3.1 percent year on year, but Bratlie said he believed the figure would come down in April with falling electricy prices.
Analysts agreed that the volatility of the crown was big because the market was thin and because the central bank has stopped intervening to stabilise the currency.
The crown at one point on Friday weakened to 4.1620 against the mark, its lowest level since late December. At 1400gmt, it had recovered to 4.1270 against the mark.
The crown was quoted at 101.26 against the inverse ECU index for a four-month low against the basket of European currencies.
On January 10, the central bank cut official interest rates for the second time in two days in a futile attempt to rein in the runaway petrocurrency.
The bank, buckling under market pressure, simultaneously announced it would now curb its massive but fruitless intervention and let the crown run its course for a while.
"The movement from 4.20 to 3.90 was so incredible you had to have a backlash," Bratlie said, recalling the crown's bull run in recent months.
John Eriksen, Scandinavian economist at London-based I.D.E.A., also believed the crown would appreciate again longer term supported by strong fundamentals.

"The crown has taken a beating over the past few sessions, and some speculation of a rate hike has emerged. In our view, the crown's move is not likely to prompt any action from the central bank yet," Eriksen said.
"For that to happen, we believe the crown would have to slide further versus the ECU index. An early warning could be some intervention to test the market," he said.
"In the short term, we see DEM/NOK resistance at 4.1720 and then at 4.1920," he said, but added that fundamentals would suggest a solid long-run backing for the crown.
Apart from the wage talks, analysts were looking for the April inflation figures to be released on May 9 and the revised national budget to be presented on May 13.

Foreign investors started buying crowns several months ago after analysts said the currency was undervalued given that the Norwegian economy was booming with huge surpluses in the national budget and current account. Norway is the world's second biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia.
Interest rate cuts fuelled speculative buying.
The central bank announced in February that it would resume purchases of foreign currency in order to manage the state's Petroleum Fund.
Norway expects to have a budget surplus of 55.4 billion crowns in 1997, all of which will be pumped into the Petroleum Fund for investment in foreign government bonds.
